topic: What if you opened a McDonald's in ancient Rome?

script.text: And that's when you remember history class.

On the night of the eighteenth of July, in the year sixty-four, a fire broke out in the shops around the Circus Maximus. The Great Fire of Rome. It burned for six days. Of the city's fourteen districts, only four were left untouched. That's real.
You're standing in a shop next to the Circus Maximus, with a grill that has to burn all night. On the eighteenth of July.
You turn to put the fire out. And the man with the purple stripe is standing in the doorway, with two soldiers. 'The emperor's feast,' he says softly. 'The grill stays lit.'
Somewhere down the street, someone shouts. And the sky over the Circus starts to glow orange.
So did you just start the Great Fire of Rome? Or did someone want it to look like you did? Tell me what you'd do, in the comments.

And is any of this real? The history is. Rome had fast food counters. A Roman cookbook has a meat patty. No tomatoes or potatoes in Europe until after fourteen ninety-two. Nero banned hot food in taverns. And the fire started at the Circus Maximus, on the eighteenth of July. What happens next? That's part two.

science.claim: The Great Fire of Rome broke out on 18/19 July AD 64 in the shops around the Circus Maximus and burned six days; of 14 districts, 4 were untouched.
science.working: Tacitus: the fire began in the part of the Circus next to the Palatine and Caelian hills, among shops with flammable goods, on 19 July (the night of 18-19 July); it raged six days before being stopped at the foot of the Esquiline. Of Rome's fourteen districts four stood intact, three were levelled and seven reduced to a few ruins.
